verses.zh: 这从以东的波斯拉来，穿红衣服，装扮华美，能力广大，大步行走的是谁呢？就是我，是凭公义说话，以大能施行拯救。
verses.en: Who is this who comes from Edom,[NOTE:1] dressed in bright red, coming from Bozrah?[NOTE:2] Who[NOTE:3] is this one wearing royal attire,[NOTE:4] who marches confidently[NOTE:5] because of his great strength?“It is I, the one who announces vindication,and who is able to deliver!”[NOTE:6]
notes: Edom is here an archetype for the Lord’s enemies. See 34:5.
Heb “[in] bright red garments, from Bozrah.”
The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis; note the first line of the verse.
Heb “honored in his clothing”; KJV, ASV “glorious in his apparel.”
The Hebrew text has צָעָה (tsaʿah), which means “stoop, bend” (51:14). The translation assumes an emendation to צָעַד (tsaʿad, “march”; see BDB 858 s.v. צָעָה).
Heb “I, [the one] speaking in vindication [or “righteousness”], great to deliver.”

verses.zh: 你的装扮为何有红色？你的衣服为何像踹酒榨的呢？
verses.en: Why are your clothes red?Why do you look like someone who has stomped on grapes in a vat?[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and your garments like one who treads in a vat?”

verses.zh: 我独自踹酒榨；众民中无一人与我同在。我发怒将他们踹下，发烈怒将他们践踏。他们的血溅在我衣服上，并且污染了我一切的衣裳。
verses.en: “I have stomped grapes in the winepress all by myself;no one from the nations joined me.I stomped on them[NOTE:1] in my anger;I trampled them down in my rage.Their juice splashed on my garmentsand stained[NOTE:2] all my clothes.
notes: Nations, headed by Edom, are the object of the Lord’s anger (see v. 6). He compares military slaughter to stomping on grapes in a vat.

Heb “and I stained.” For discussion of the difficult verb form, see HALOT 170 s.v. II גאל. Perhaps the form is mixed, combining the first person forms of the imperfect (note the alef prefix) and perfect (note the תי- ending).

verses.zh: 因为，报仇之日在我心中；救赎我民之年已经来到。
verses.en: For I looked forward to the day of vengeance,and then payback time arrived.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “for the day of vengeance was in my heart, and the year of my revenge came.” The term גְּאוּלַי (geʾulay) is sometimes translated here “my redemption,” for the verbal root גאל often means “deliver, buy back.” A גֹּאֵל (goʾel, “kinsman-redeemer”) was responsible for protecting the extended family’s interests, often by redeeming property that had been sold outside the family. However, the responsibilities of a גֹּאֵל extended beyond financial concerns. He was also responsible for avenging the shed blood of a family member (see Num 35:19-27; Deut 19:6-12). In Isa 63:4, where vengeance is a prominent theme (note the previous line), it is probably this function of the family protector that is in view. The Lord pictures himself as a blood avenger who waits for the day of vengeance to arrive and then springs into action.

verses.zh: 我仰望，见无人帮助；我诧异，没有人扶持。所以，我自己的膀臂为我施行拯救；我的烈怒将我扶持。
verses.en: I looked, but there was no one to help;I was shocked because there was no one offering support.[NOTE:1] So my right arm accomplished deliverance;my raging anger drove me on.[NOTE:2]
notes: See Isa 59:16 for similar language.
Heb “and my anger, it supported me”; NIV “my own wrath sustained me.”

verses.zh: 我发怒，踹下众民；发烈怒，使他们沉醉，又将他们的血倒在地上。
verses.en: I trampled nations in my anger;I made them drunk[NOTE:1] in my rage;I splashed their blood on the ground.”[NOTE:2]
notes: See Isa 49:26 and 51:23 for similar imagery.
Heb “and I brought down to the ground their juice.” “Juice” refers to their blood (see v. 3).

verses.zh: 我要照耶和华一切所赐给我们的，提起他的慈爱和美德，并他向以色列家所施的大恩；这恩是照他的怜恤和丰盛的慈爱赐给他们的。
verses.en: I will tell of the faithful acts of the Lord,of the Lord’s praiseworthy deeds.I will tell about all[NOTE:1] the Lord did for us,the many good things he did for the family of Israel,[NOTE:2] because of[NOTE:3] his compassion and great faithfulness.
notes: Heb “according to all which.”
Heb “greatness of goodness to the house of Israel which he did for them.”
Heb “according to.”

verses.zh: 他说：他们诚然是我的百姓，不行虚假的子民；这样，他就作了他们的救主。
verses.en: He said, “Certainly they will be my people,children who are not disloyal.”[NOTE:1] He became their deliverer.
notes: Heb “children [who] do not act deceitfully.” Here the verb refers to covenantal loyalty.

verses.zh: 他们在一切苦难中，他也同受苦难；并且他面前的使者拯救他们；他以慈爱和怜悯救赎他们；在古时的日子常保抱他们，怀搋他们。
verses.en: Through all that they suffered, he suffered too.[NOTE:1] The messenger sent from his very presence[NOTE:2] delivered them.In his love and mercy he protected[NOTE:3] them;he lifted them up and carried them throughout ancient times.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “in all their distress, there was distress to him” (reading לוֹ [lo] with the margin/Qere).

This may refer to the “angel of God” mentioned in Exod 14:19, who in turn may be identical to the divine “presence” (literally, “face”) referred to in Exod 33:14-15 and Deut 4:37. Here in Isa 63 this messenger may be equated with God’s “holy Spirit” (see vv. 10-11) and “the Spirit of the Lord” (v. 14). See also Ps 139:7, where God’s “Spirit” seems to be equated with his “presence” (literally, “face”) in the synonymous parallelistic structure.tn Heb “the messenger [or “angel”] of his face”; NIV “the angel of his presence.”
Or “redeemed” (KJV, NAB, NIV), or “delivered.”
Heb “all the days of antiquity”; KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV “days of old.”

verses.zh: 他们竟悖逆，使主的圣灵担忧。他就转作他们的仇敌，亲自攻击他们。
verses.en: But they rebelled and offended[NOTE:1] his Holy Spirit,[NOTE:2] so he turned into an enemyand fought against them.
notes: Or “grieved, hurt the feelings of.”
The phrase “Holy Spirit” occurs in the OT only here (in v. 11 as well) and in Ps 51:11 (51:13 HT), where it is associated with the divine presence.

verses.zh: 那时，他们（原文是他）想起古时的日子―摩西和他百姓，说：将百姓和牧养他全群的人从海里领上来的在哪里呢？将他的圣灵降在他们中间的在哪里呢？
verses.en: His people remembered the ancient times.[NOTE:1] Where is the one who brought them up out of the sea,along with the shepherd of[NOTE:2] his flock?Where is the one who placed his Holy Spirit among them,[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and he remembered the days of antiquity, Moses, his people.” The syntax of the statement is unclear. The translation assumes that “his people” is the subject of the verb “remembered.” If original, “Moses” is in apposition to “the days of antiquity,” more precisely identifying the time period referred to. However, the syntactical awkwardness suggests that “Moses” may have been an early marginal note (perhaps identifying “the shepherd of his flock” two lines later) that has worked its way into the text.

The Hebrew text has a plural form, which if retained and taken as a numerical plural, would probably refer to Moses, Aaron, and the Israelite tribal leaders at the time of the Exodus. Most prefer to emend the form to the singular (רָעָה, raʿah) and understand this as a reference just to Moses.
See the note at v. 10.

verses.zh: 使他荣耀的膀臂在摩西的右手边行动，在他们前面将水分开，要建立自己永远的名，
verses.en: the one who made his majestic power available to Moses,[NOTE:1] who divided the water before them,gaining for himself a lasting reputation,[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “who caused to go at the right hand of Moses the arm of his splendor.”
Heb “making for himself a lasting name.”

verses.zh: 带领他们经过深处，如马行走旷野，使他们不致绊跌的在哪里呢？
verses.en: who led them through the deep water?Like a horse running through the wilderness[NOTE:1] they did not stumble.
notes: Heb “in the desert [or “steppe”].”

verses.zh: 耶和华的灵使他们得安息，彷佛牲畜下到山谷；照样，你也引导你的百姓，要建立自己荣耀的名。
verses.en: As an animal that goes down into a valley to graze,[NOTE:1] so the Spirit of the Lord granted them rest.In this way[NOTE:2] you guided your people,gaining for yourself an honored reputation.[NOTE:3]
notes: The words “to graze” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Or “so” (KJV, ASV), or “thus” (NAB, NRSV).
Heb “making for yourself a majestic name.”

verses.zh: 求你从天上垂顾，从你圣洁荣耀的居所观看。你的热心和你大能的作为在哪里呢？你爱慕的心肠和怜悯向我们止住了。
verses.en: Look down from heaven and take notice,from your holy, majestic palace!Where are your zeal[NOTE:1] and power?Do not hold back your tender compassion![NOTE:2]
notes: This probably refers to his zeal for his people, which motivates him to angrily strike out against their enemies.

The Hebrew text reads literally, “the agitation of your intestines and your compassion to me they are held back.” The phrase “agitation of your intestines” is metonymic, referring to the way in which one’s nervous system reacts when one feels pity and compassion toward another. אֵלַי (ʾelay, “to me”) is awkward in this context, where the speaker represents the nation and, following the introduction (see v. 7), utilizes first person plural forms. The translation assumes an emendation to the negative particle אַל (ʾal). This also necessitates emending the following verb form (which is a plural perfect) to a singular jussive (תִתְאַפָּק, titʾappaq). The Hitpael of אָפַק (ʾafaq) also occurs in 42:14.

verses.zh: 亚伯拉罕虽然不认识我们，以色列也不承认我们，你却是我们的父。耶和华啊，你是我们的父；从万古以来，你名称为「我们的救赎主」。
verses.en: For you are our father,though Abraham does not know usand Israel does not recognize us.You, Lord, are our father;you have been called our Protector from ancient times.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “our protector [or “redeemer”] from antiquity [is] your name.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，你为何使我们走差离开你的道，使我们心里刚硬、不敬畏你呢？求你为你仆人，为你产业支派的缘故，转回来。
verses.en: Why, Lord, do you make us stray[NOTE:1] from your ways[NOTE:2] and make our minds stubborn so that we do not obey you?[NOTE:3] Return for the sake of your servants,the tribes of your inheritance!
notes: Some suggest a tolerative use of the Hiphil here, “[why do] you allow us to stray?” (cf. NLT). Though the Hiphil of תָעָה (taʿah) appears to be tolerative in Jer 50:6, elsewhere it is preferable or necessary to take it as causative. See Isa 3:12; 9:15; and 30:28, as well as Gen 20:13; 2 Kgs 21:9; Job 12:24-25; Prov 12:26; Jer 23:13, 32; Hos 4:12; Amos 2:4; Mic 3:5.
This probably refers to God’s commands.

Heb “[Why do] you harden our heart[s] so as not to fear you.” The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).sn How direct this hardening is, one cannot be sure. The speaker may envision direct involvement on the Lord’s part. The Lord has brought the exile as judgment for the nation’s sin and now he continues to keep them at arm’s length by blinding them spiritually. The second half of 64:7 might support this, though the precise reading of the final verb is uncertain. On the other hand, the idiom of lament is sometimes ironic and hyperbolically deterministic. For example, Naomi lamented that Shaddai was directly opposing her and bringing her calamity (Ruth 1:20-21), while the author of Ps 88 directly attributes his horrible suffering and loneliness to God (see especially vv. 6-8, 16-18). Both individuals make little, if any, room for intermediate causes or the principle of sin and death which ravages the human race. In the same way, the speaker in Isa 63:17 (who evidences great spiritual sensitivity and is anything but “hardened”) may be referring to the hardships of exile, which discouraged and even embittered the people, causing many of them to retreat from their Yahwistic faith. In this case, the “hardening” in view is more indirect and can be lifted by the Lord’s intervention. Whether the hardening here is indirect or direct, it is important to recognize that the speaker sees it as one of the effects of rebellion against the Lord (note especially 64:5-6).

verses.zh: 你的圣民不过暂时得这产业；我们的敌人已经践踏你的圣所。
verses.en: For a short time your special[NOTE:1] nation possessed a land,[NOTE:2] but then our adversaries knocked down[NOTE:3] your holy sanctuary.
notes: Or “holy” (ASV, NASB, NRSV, TEV, NLT).
Heb “for a short time they had a possession, the people of your holiness.”
Heb “your adversaries trampled on.”

verses.zh: 我们好像你未曾治理的人，又像未曾得称你名下的人。
verses.en: We existed from ancient times,[NOTE:1] but you did not rule over them;they were not your subjects.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “we were from antiquity” (see v. 16). The collocation of הָיָה, מִן, and עוֹלָם (hayah, min, and ʿolam) occurs only here.

Heb “you did not rule them; your name was not called over them.” The expression “the name is called over” indicates ownership; see the note at 4:1. As these two lines stand, they are very difficult to interpret. They appear to be stating that the adversaries just mentioned in v. 18 have not been subject to the Lord’s rule in the past, perhaps explaining why they could commit the atrocity described in v. 18b.
